content.title: Leveraging the Variance of Return Sequences for Exploration Policy
content.review:
This paper is well-written in terms of the English, but unfortunately the authors make a simple error that invalidates the results of the paper.

There are two major notions of uncertainty that must be considered in statistics (and RL). So-called 'aleatoric' or irreducible, and 'epistemic' or reducible. Aleatoric is the intrinsic uncertainty / randomness in the system, for example when flipping a coin with Prob(heads) = p it will always have some randomness about the outcome (heads vs tails) - this uncertainty is irreducible. Epistemic uncertainty on the other hand is the agents own (possibly Bayesian) uncertainty about the parameters of the system, for example when flipping a coin the agent should be able to know p with greater certainty the more data the agent observes - this uncertainty is reducible, since more data should reduce it.

The type of uncertainty that can be used for exploration is epistemic. Aleatoric uncertainty yields almost no insight into the agent's epistemic uncertainty (I say almost because the aleatoric uncertainty influences the epistemic uncertainty, in that systems with higher intrinsic randomness are harder to learn about, eg, the posterior will concentrate slower, but to first order of approximation this separation is correct). As a concrete example consider a two-armed multi-armed bandit, where arm A has a lower average reward than arm B but significantly higher reward *variance*. In this case the aleatoric uncertainty of arm A is higher, but that tells us nothing about the agent's uncertainty about the average reward. The algorithm of this paper would pull arm A significantly more than it should, since it is prioritizing aleatoric uncertainty.  I think this case is made clearly in the Uncertainty Bellman Equation work: https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.05380, which seems like prior work that should be cited. In that paper the authors explicitly consider epistemic uncertainty, and show that the 'variance' of this uncertainty satisfies a Bellman equation. This is the correct notion of variance that can be used for exploration.

In this paper the authors confuse the two uncertainties. They use aleatoric to drive exploration, which isn't correct. As a thought exercise - how would the algorithm in this paper solve the DeepSea environment in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.03568.pdf ? This very simple environment can be thought of as an exploration 'unit test', and this algorithm would fail. The numerical experiments also drive home the fact that this is not exploring efficiently. In the hard exploration problems from table 1 here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.01310.pdf, this algorithm tends to do poorly (eg Montezuma's revenge, pitfall, venture etc.).

Ultimately this paper should not be published in its current form.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response from the authors
content.comment:
First of all, we want to thank you for bringing up this important issue in exploration. We fully understand your concern about the source of uncertainty. And we acknowledge that the stochastic property of the system or the environment, if exists, does weaken our methods. Generally, aleatoric uncertainty poses a common challenge for most of the exploration methods built on bonuses of uncertainty or curiosity, such as noisy networks, curiosity-driven exploration etc.. But those methods can still be useful when aleatoric one doesn't dominate the overall uncertainty. Though the methods we propose here don't particularly solve this problem, they don't necessarily suffer from it more significantly than the other methods of this type. If we consider a situation that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties have a similar impact on the magnitude of change, the variances of return sequences capture epistemic uncertainty more than aleatoric one. Our empirical analysis in the appendix, along with the policy iteration proof in Sutton's book, shows that Q value function generally improves monotonically. While the irreducible errors usually vibrate, the variances are generally higher for monotonic sequences when they have similar magnitudes of change. And of course, the Q-value function doesn't improve strictly monotonically in Monto Carlo configurations. But we observe that the magnitude of change caused by sampling is generally greater than that from other sources. Therefore, if limiting the system or environment to those where aleatoric uncertainty doesn't dominate, our methods can work well. While this is an important issue, we will add a few paragraphs in the paper to discuss it.

To further address this problem, as well as alleviate the cold-start problem we mentioned in the discussion section, we are working on alternative methods that introducing randomness to states with high variance, which has a similar underlying idea of noisy networks, rather than preferring action-states with high variance directly. It can be achieved by, for example, changing "pi(s) = argmax(Q(s,a) + sigma(s,a) x c)" to "pi(s) = argmax(Q(s,a) + sigma(s,a) x c x e)" where "e" is sampled from uniform or Gaussian distribution. With this modification, the bonuses have zero expectations while they impact the behaviors in a more stochastic way. We will add the method and results if we are able to complete the experiments by the revision deadline. Experimenting on numerous Atari games makes us a bit short of resource and makes each run of experiments slow.

Additionally, the improvement on performance is overall better than it looks in the figures. We believe that the confusion is because our methods outperform a few games dramatically and those scores enlarge the scale of y-axes, which makes the other improvement nearly invisible. As reviewer \#3 suggested, we updated Figure 2 and Figure 3 with logarithmic scales in the revision.

Overall, we explore the possibility of utilizing the variances of return sequences as an information source to guide exploration, and show it works reasonably well empirically. We don't expect it alone to be able to work well in highly stochastic environments. And as a local method, it has a limited capability on deep exploration compared to Uncertainty Bellman Equation or Bootstrapped DQN. Nevertheless, we believe it is worth to be brought up while it is a missing piece in the map, and appeal for further exploration.

content.comment: Thank you for responding. However, I remain unconvinced about the soundness of this approach. I don't fully understand your response, but one counter-point I have is that if you have a fixed stochastic policy in an MDP that will induce randomness in the returns from any state, and this is actually a source of _aleatoric_ uncertainty, not epistemic. I also object to the notion that curiosity-driven exploration suffers as much as this from aleatoric uncertainty (I'm not as sure about noisy nets). Curiosity driven exploration is a very ambiguous term and could mean almost anything, but if we take the semi-standard definition of learning a predictive model of next state / observation and using the errors as a bonus then it's clear that epistemic uncertainty is the primary driving factor, not aleatoric.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
There might be a misunderstanding of aleatoric uncertainty between us. We assume that aleatoric uncertainty (or stochastic property of the environments) can be of multiple forms, where stochastic reward function and stochastic state transition function are two different examples. For the latter, if an exploration strategy uses the errors of predicting the next state/observation as a bonus, which I referred to as curiosity-driven methods in the former response, it will suffer from the aleatoric uncertainty.

But according to your response, we assume that you concern more about the impact of aleatoric uncertainty on the rewards. And in the former response, we justify that this impact is limited and not necessarily more serious for our methods, especially in the environments where aleatoric uncertainty doesn't dominate. In addition, we compare our methods to Noisy Networks and Prioritized Experience Replay here to further clarify our justification:

1) Our methods are different from noisy networks in two major ways: a) noisy networks use additional neural network parameters (or weights) to implicitly estimate the uncertainty of predicting the rewards (or returns), while our methods estimate it explicitly with an additional stream; b) during exploration, noisy networks pick the actions more randomly in the states of high uncertainty of predicting rewards/returns, while our methods use the uncertainty of predicting rewards/returns for each single actions as bonuses and add them on top of the predicted rewards in those states.

2) Prioritized Experience Replay shares a similar underlying idea of our methods to use the uncertainty of predicting rewards/returns as a bonus. The major difference is that it uses the bonus to sample from experience for updating the predictive model in spite of how the experience is gained, while our methods use the bonus to guide exploration and gain experience.

Neither the above methods nor our methods is able to distinguish aleatoric uncertainty from epistemic one, which makes all of them assign learning or exploration budget unreasonably if the rewards are highly stochastic. Empirically, they can still be useful and valuable in less stochastic environments. Moreover, as all those methods are essentially TD(0) algorithms, the stochastic property is stabilized and alleviated by constructing returns on estimations of the next states.

While performing in stochastic environments is an important challenge and our methods don't particularly deal with it, we believe that they can be extended to address it. For example, there is a possibility to have an additional method, such as [1], to analyze the source of uncertainty in the rewards, and apply the adjusted rewards on our methods.

We respond with a long text to clarify our ideas and hopefully, it won't cause too much trouble on your time.

[1] Wang et. al., "Reinforcement Learning with Perturbed Rewards", arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.01032(2018).

content.title: Review
content.review:
# Summary 
This paper proposes to estimate the variance of the return using a neural network and use the estimated variance as an exploration bonus when acting in RL. Specifically, the paper presents two ways to measure uncertainty: 1) the exponentially weighted standard deviation of return or 2) the TD-error. The empirical results on Atari games show that the proposed exploration policy outperforms $\epsilon$-greedy policy when applied to Double DQN (DDQN). 

Pros
* The performance is (slightly) better than the baseline. 

Cons
* Lack of theoretical analysis
* Lack of comparison to other uncertainty measures
* Lack of empirical analysis

# Novelty
* The idea of using TD-error as a measure for learning progress has been discussed in the context of experience replay, which is for learning. Using such information for generating exploratory behavior is new to my knowledge. 

# Quality
* The results on Atari games seem to indicate that the proposed method works better than $\epsilon$-greedy policy in practice, though the improvement seems a bit marginal. 
* My major concern is that this paper does not have any theoretical analysis of the proposed method unlike the other theoretically well-grounded exploration approaches (e.g., count-based method). For example, it is unclear whether the proposed method guarantees convergence.
* The proposed method uncertainty measure does not seem to isolate the uncertainty of Q-estimation from the uncertainty of the environment dynamics. For example, if the environment has a highly stochastic reward function, the variance of return will be always large, which will be always encouraged according to the proposed method. On the other hand, many other exploration approaches (e.g., bootstrapped DQN, count-based exploration) won’t have such a problem.
* Related to the above, it would be important to compare the proposed method to other uncertainty measures (e.g., bootstrapped DQN, model uncertainty, etc) and show the unique benefit of the proposed method.
* It would be good to show some empirical analysis showing when the proposed method helps or hurts. The current set of empirical results is not so comprehensive. 

# Clarity
The paper is easy to follow.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Needs comparisons with other recent work in exploration
content.review:
## Summary

A challenge in reinforcement learning is how to explore effectively. In small tabular state and action spaces good solutions exist such as Upper Confidence Bound. However, it is non-trivial to determine how to scale such approaches to large state and action spaces.

The approach taken here is to add an additional ``head'' to a DQN network which tracks (using a TD estimator) the variance of returns for each state and action (as well as the standard predictions of the return for each action with the other head) (the empirical returns are weighted to emphasize recent returns when estimating variance) [this is what the paper states, as elaborated below I'm not sure this is quite correct]. Then the policy followed during training is $\pi(s) = \argmax_a \hat{Q}(s, a) + c \hat{\sigma}(s, a)$ where $\hat{Q}$ is the value prediction and $\hat{\sigma}$ is the variance prediction, $c$ is a hyper-parameter. This is a particular form of "optimism in uncertainty" in that actions which have had high variance outcomes are valued more highly.

They provide some simple experiments for the tabular case and then experiments on Atari showing significant improvements over Double DQN baselines.

## Feedback

Describing the method and in the tabular experiments it seems the variance of returns is used for $\sigma$. But in the actual scalable algorithm the "variance" of the return is estimated using the TD(0) error (algorithm 1 shows this most clearly). This seems a significant limitation because it means that it lacks what Bootstrap DQN refers to as ``deep'' exploration. If a state has high variance outcomes then good exploration may require navigating again to this state, but the TD(0) error may even be 0 on states leading to the unexplored state. Stated another way, the TD(0) estimate of returns has high bias, which will lead to substantially underestimating the true variance of the returns. This concern should be discussed.

I was unable to follow how the variance estimation in section 4.1 is incorporated. It's not mentioned in the algorithm 1 or the losses in eq 8-11.

The "noisy-TV" (explained in [1]) problem for exploration, where an agent may repeatedly visit states with stochastic outcomes even when no further learning is possible is a challenge in exploration. This issue should be discussed (I believe the approach discussed here will fall for a noisy TV) and ideally experiments in a stochastic environment should be included.

One significant limitation of the empirical experiments on Atari is the lack of comparison with more challenging alternative approaches to exploration such as RND [2] which significant outperforms on some of the hard-exploration tasks such as Montezuma's revenge (here there is almost no gain on this over DDQN baseline), [3, 4] which also have substantial gains over many of the hard exploration Atari tasks here ([1] is a nice reference on recent work in exploration for Deep RL). Many of the Atari tasks typically considered to be exploration challenges are not improved over DDQN here and this should be discussed.

I found it confusing in the abstract and elsewhere to refer to constructing an "upper bound." This would seem to imply some theoretical guarantee or at least argument that an upper bound is being approximated somewhere. However, the method is heuristic and there is no particular guarantee that it is the upper bound of the true return, particularly given the variance is estimated using TD(0). There is even a hyperparameter for how much to scale the variance by when estimating value.

# Conclusion

Overall I think this work is interesting but not very theoretically well justified and although there are gains over DDQN baseline, as far as can easily be compared, there is not really gains over other recent work in exploration. For this reason I think this work may be of limited interest.

[1] https://lilianweng.github.io/lil-log/2020/06/07/exploration-strategies-in-deep-reinforcement-learning.html#exploration-via-disagreement

[2] Burda, Yuri, et al. "Exploration by random network distillation." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.12894 (2018).

[3] Badia, Adrià Puigdomènech, et al. "Never Give Up: Learning Directed Exploration Strategies." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.06038 (2020).

[4] Ecoffet, Adrien, et al. "First return then explore." arXiv preprint arXiv:2004.12919 (2020).

content.title: Review and Questions
content.review:
This paper proposes two new value-based methods to improve exploration. The two techniques improve exploration using the variance in the 1) return sequence and 2) weighted TD error. This work also contributes a two-head neural network to estimate the Q-value and the variance as well as optimization improvements. 

It's interesting to drive the exploration directly from rewards, rather than observations or states as most exploration methods recommend. I believe the clarity of the work could be improved and I would increase my score upon improvement in clarity and satisfactory answers to my questions.

Questions to authors:
* The largest improvements of your exploration method come for games that present no exploration difficulty, refer to Ali Taiga et al, (2019) for a list of hard/easy exploration games. We are finding little-to-no improvement on difficult exploration games like Montezuma’s Revenge, PrivateEye, Venture.
* The premise is that variance of the value of a state-action pair can be used to estimate the convergence speed of the value function for that state-action. However, if the environment is simply very stochastic from that point, won’t this upweight these states? Does this fail the Schmidhuber noisy-TV test?
* Can you describe how you ensured strong baselines? I’ve noticed that on many tasks that the performance is below that achieved by agents in Dopamine [https://google.github.io/dopamine/baselines/plots.html].


Notes:
* The clarity of the paper can be improved. As one instance, “During Monte Carlo policy evaluation… This series can start diverging due to the cyclic nature of value-based approaches; the evolving value function begets policy improvements which in turn modify the value function” -- under policy evaluation, the value function does not evolve. What is going on here?
* Please make the separate sigma-stream more explicit earlier [Section 4.1]. Diagram in appendix perhaps?
* I’d recommend logarithmic axes for Figure 2 and Figure 3. The dramatically different scores mask the improvements. A reader might look at this and conclude that while these methods improve, sometimes considerably, on several games, that they actually hurt performance on as much as 40% of games.
* Nit:  It’s redundant to say you’re introducing a novel method -- just say you’re introducing a method.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Thank you for the positive review and valuable suggestions!

Regarding the concern that the largest improvements come from easier exploration games instead of hard ones, there are two possible reasons: 1) The current form of our methods is essentially a local one, which might not perform exceptionally in sparse-reward environments which usually requires "deep" exploration. However, the weighted variance of return sequence is a valuable and missing information source from current reinforcement learning literature. We explore the possibility as well as show its value in this paper. And we believe that it can be extended to address further challenges. 2) The value of our parameter "c" has an impact on the exploration behaviors, especially in the games with sparser rewards. We tuned it based on the overall normalized scores without paying too much attention on a specific subset of the games. Meanwhile, the harder games usually have a lower normalized score base, which makes our choice of "c" prefer the easier games. With a limited time of rebuttal phrase, we are unable to re-tune it. But we believe it is partially responsible for this issue.

Regarding the concern about stochastic environment, please refer to the first paragraph of our response to reviewer \#4. (We tried quoting it here but it made our response exceed word limit.)

For the noisy-TV test, it's hard to simply say our methods would succeed or fail. An environment with highly stochastic observations poses a challenge for the exploration methods preferably seeking new experiences, such as curiosity-driven methods. While our methods learn from rewards directly, the key for them to work in this type of test is the design of the reward function. Imagine that if the reward is set to 0 or a low value when the observation satisfies some conditions that decide it's less of interest, our exploration methods drive the agent away without any difficulty.

Regarding the concern about the baseline, we have to admit that it is not the strongest as we implement all the components from scratch and simply follow the hyper-parameters in Rainbow DQN paper and Prioritized Experience Replay paper. However, to avoid any bias in that, we obtain all the reported results, including the baselines, with the same implementation and configuration, except for the unique parts of the methods. Also, the baseline scores are at least as good as those reported in references, such as Prioritized Experience Replay paper or Rainbow DQN paper. Therefore, we are confident that it's a fair comparison. (By the way, the link to Dopamine provided in the review is invalid.)

Your suggestions are very valuable.
Two of the reviewers indeed have doubts about the improvements, probably because of the figures. We have had them updated to logarithmic scale and they look more clear now.

Regarding the clarity example, we express the update of value function and the update of policy separately and show the cyclic nature by describing the alternates between those two updating process. The value function is updated only once in each turn of policy evaluation, and we use the term "evolve" to show the process of these updates in its multiple turns. Please let us know if the sentences in the paper convey the message accurately, and we can rephrase it if not.

Variance estimation itself (Section 4.1) is a general method that doesn't involve any neural networks. And it's presented as a separate function from Q-value function. We assume that you suggest giving a diagram to show the architecture of the two-stream neural networks (Section 4.2). That's a great suggestion and we will add one along with a description in the following revisions.

Also, we will update the abstract without the "novel" word as you make a good point to make the writing concise.
